prime.problem: pass@100 assumes something tells you which of the 100 programs works. In an editor with no tests, you have to choose one blind, and a random pick throws away most of what the extra samples bought.
prime.fits: The bridge from pass@k (oracle picks) to deployment (you pick). It uses the samples produced by temperature and nucleus sampling and the log-probs the model already computed.
expect: mean vs sum of token log-probs
prime.goal: Rank samples by mean log-probability by hand, explain why the sum fails, and say how much of the oracle's advantage ranking recovers.

attend: Why does summing log-probs systematically prefer shorter programs?
What does dividing by length turn the score into, in terms of a 'typical token'?
Why is this heuristic free compared with back-translation ranking?
What kind of wrong program will this ranking happily pick first?

must: Every token's log-prob is ≤ 0 → summing penalises every extra token → sum ranks by brevity → can do slightly worse than random
Divide by length → score becomes the average per-token confidence → length cancels → picks the sample the model is most consistently sure of → +11.6 points over random for Codex-S on average
Log-probs come out of generation anyway → ranking needs no tests, no second model, no extra pass → the cheapest usable 'generate many, show one' recipe
Model confidence ≠ correctness → confidently wrong code ranks high → 44.5% vs the oracle's 77.5%, so where tests exist, running them beats ranking
elevated: Ranking gain grows with sample count up to the budget → but so does generation cost → 100 samples per suggestion is a heavy price for 6.8 points at 12B
reference: the illustrative log-probs in the worked example
+11.6 as a cross-size average for Codex-S

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3 sentences how to pick one of k samples without tests, why the mean beats the sum, and where it lands between random and the oracle for Codex-S-12B.
checklist: score each sample by its mean per-token log-probability; return the top one
the sum penalises length, so it picks short samples
Codex-S-12B, 100 samples: random 37.7%, mean log-prob 44.5%, oracle 77.5%

retrieve.q: Explain why a ranking heuristic is needed at all, when pass@100 already shows the model can solve 77.5% of problems.
answer: pass@100 assumes an oracle picks the passing sample
a user without tests needs one program chosen automatically
a random pick only gets pass@1 (37.7%)

retrieve.q: Walk through scoring sample A (5 tokens, sum −1.00) and sample B (20 tokens, each −0.15) under sum and mean. Which does each pick, and why?
answer: B's typical token is more likely (e^−0.15 ≈ 0.861 vs e^−0.2 ≈ 0.819)

retrieve.q: Ranking recovers how much of the gap between a random sample and the oracle for Codex-S-12B? Is that worth 100 generations per suggestion?
answer: a real gain over random, but far from the oracle
worth it only if latency and compute allow; tests, where available, do much better

compare.q: Mean log-prob and back-translation both rank samples without tests. What signal does each use, and why does the paper prefer the simpler one?
answer: mean log-prob: the generator's own per-token confidence
back-translation: P(docstring | sample) under a second model
back-translation needs another model and extra passes, overfits quickly, and scores lower

compare.q: On APPS the paper filters by the 3 public example tests; here it ranks by log-prob. What does each selection signal know about correctness, and which wins when both are available?
answer: example tests check real behaviour on a few inputs
the paper says filtering by public tests beats every log-prob heuristic

predict.q: Add sample C: 10 tokens, each with log-prob −0.25. Rank A, B and C by sum and by mean. Does adding C change which sample either rule picks? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: C's sum is −2.50 and its mean −0.250. By sum: A (−1.00) > C (−2.50) > B (−3.00), so the sum still picks A. By mean: B (−0.150) > A (−0.200) > C (−0.250), so the mean still picks B. Neither pick changes, but C shows the sum's order simply follows length.

apply.task: Design a tiny experiment: take 5 problems you can test, generate 10 samples each from any code model, and record each sample's mean and summed log-prob. Compare the pass rate of (a) a random sample, (b) the top mean-log-prob sample, (c) the top summed-log-prob sample, (d) any passing sample.
apply.done: You have a 4-row table for your 5 problems and can say whether your ordering matches the paper's: oracle > mean > random, with the sum near or below random.
apply.hint: If you can't run a model, do it on paper: invent log-probs for 3 samples per problem where the shortest is wrong, and show the sum picks it.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether sample C changes either pick?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the sum can be worse than random?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: confidence → correctness, or length → sum bias?
Did 17% of the gap feel smaller than you expected from the headline numbers?
What will you check in the Codex-D card: why a second model doesn't beat this?
